newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Analysts still expect Ivory Coast-IMF deal soon.
newsitem.headline: Analysts still expect Ivory Coast-IMF deal soon.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund and Ivory Coast failed to agree on a new structural adjustment programme at talks here last week, but bank analysts were optimistic a deal would be clinched soon.

Analysts were reassured Ivory Coast had agreed to commodity reforms, including the complete reform of the Caistab commodities marketing board, seen as a potential stumbling block since the government had resisted it for so long.
"I was a bit worried that the Caistab was going to hamstring the whole deal. Frankly, I'm surprised that anything else was able to stop a deal," said one London-based analyst.
He was confident there would be an agreement soon.
"The IMF and World Bank consider Ivory Coast as one of their pet projects," he said.

They agreed extensive loans after the 50 percent devaluation of the CFA franc in 1994, and economic results since have been impressive, with seven percent growth in both 1995 and 1996 and inflation kept under control.
Similar confidence was expressed by another banking analyst.

"If the problem had been over the Caistab, I would have been worried, but it looks like the big issues have been sorted out," he said, describing even issues such as poverty reduction as "wrapping paper" by comparison.

One donor source said a deal was "extremely unlikely" to be ready for the next IMF board meeting to approve in September, but analysts said one might be concluded later that month on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings in Hong Kong.

Securing an IMF Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility is vital if Ivory Coast is to get a further rescheduling of its official Paris Club debt and for kick-starting an agreed debt reduction package with the London Club of commercial banks.

According to government documents, servicing external debt costs Ivory Coast over 63 percent of fiscal revenue. Its 1997 budget was drawn up on the basis of Paris and London Club deals reducing debt service obligations by around 40.5 billion CFA francs this year to 609.3 billion ($1 billion).

Ivory Coast, the world's biggest producer of cocoa, has agreed to reform the role of the Caistab, freeing marketing prices and leaving the private sector to take charge of export auctions for coffee and cocoa from 1999 at the latest.

The prices paid to peasant farmers are likely to go up as a result of the reforms, going some way to alleviating rural poverty in Ivory Coast, one of the donors' main concerns along with a lack of transparency in the state budget.

The Paris-based Jeune Afrique magazine reported this month that donors had insisted on parachuting two "advisers" -- one a former Ivorian minister, the other a French World Bank official -- into the finance ministry to keep an eye on the budget.
It said a lack of budget rigour was blocking an IMF deal.

However, the government says it is tackling the problem -- sifting non-existent civil servants from its payrolls, reducing the number of contract workers, often hired at the whim of section heads, and suspending officials accused of corruption.
It has also handed over the management of its debt, plus the management of operations co-funded by donors, to the Treasury as part of a move to a unified state budget.

In an interview in the same Jeune Afrique magazine, Prime Minister Daniel Kablan Duncan insisted that wage costs had been kept down and said that lower-than-expected tax revenue in the first four months of the year had been made up by end-June. ($ = 610 CFA francs)
